title: Motor development disorders in children
intro: Children learn to sit, crawl, walk, grasp and run at different rates, but some have clear delays or difficulties with movement and coordination. Motor development disorders can affect play, school and self-esteem. Early assessment and therapy help many children catch up or manage better.

sections.heading: Normal development
paragraphs: Most babies lift their heads in the first months, roll over, sit unsupported around six to nine months, crawl or shuffle, and take first steps between about nine and eighteen months. Fine motor skills such as grasping, drawing and using cutlery develop over the preschool years. There is a wide range of normal.

sections.heading: Signs of concern
paragraphs: Possible warning signs include not walking by about eighteen months, very floppy or stiff muscles, using only one side of the body, loss of skills, persistent clumsiness, frequent falling, difficulties with tying shoes, handwriting or ball games beyond what peers can do, and avoiding physical activities. Premature birth and some medical conditions raise risk.

sections.heading: Causes and assessment
paragraphs: Causes include prematurity, brain injury at birth, genetic or muscle conditions, and conditions such as developmental coordination disorder, where no clear cause is found. A paediatrician examines the child, looks at hearing, vision and growth and may refer to neurologists or specialised developmental centres. Standard tests assess motor skills and exclude other conditions.

sections.heading: Therapy and support
paragraphs: Physiotherapy and occupational therapy build strength, balance, coordination and daily living skills through play-based exercises. Practising specific tasks is most effective. Aids such as special pencil grips or supports can help, and therapists advise parents on home activities. For some neurological conditions, medicines or orthopaedic care are added.

sections.heading: Helping at home and school
paragraphs: Encourage active play, running, climbing and ball games without pressure. Ask teachers for patience, extra time and alternatives in sports. Focus on strengths and praise progress, since children with motor problems may feel embarrassed or avoid group activities.

examples.title: Raising concerns
examples.text: Imagine your two-year-old is not yet walking and falls often. You could note what they can and cannot do, bring a video to the paediatrician and ask about referral for assessment.

examples.title: Supporting at school
examples.text: Suppose your eight-year-old struggles with handwriting. You might discuss options with the teacher, such as larger paper, pencil grips, extra time or using a keyboard.
